_model: TOPIC-DRIVEN (like the daily game's menu). This blueprint holds each subject's exam FORMAT + a TOPIC OUTLINE with source GROUNDING. The dedicated generator writes exam-format questions AGAINST these topics, grounded in the grounding/src, then the validator gates them (EXAM-REVISION.md). It does NOT store final questions — generation is unlimited and ledger-steered by topic id.
_scope: English and Maths done (excluded). Covers the remaining examined subjects: Science, History, Geography, PDHPE, Commerce, Food Technology.

topic_schema.grounding: the facts/model-answer essence the generator must stay faithful to
topic_schema.exemplar: one example question (style guide, not the only question)

sections.name: Part A — Chemistry of New Substances

topics.grounding: Physical change: no new substance, often reversible (melt/boil/dissolve/change state). Chemical change: new substance, usually not reversible. FOUR indicators: colour change; gas/bubbles; precipitate forms; temperature change (heat/light). Examples: burning=chemical, boiling water=physical, boiling egg=chemical, dissolving sugar=physical.
topics.exemplar: Classify as physical or chemical: burning a match; boiling water; boiling an egg.

topics.grounding: Reactants -> products. Patterns: fuel + oxygen -> carbon dioxide + water; metal + oxygen -> metal oxide (magnesium + oxygen -> magnesium oxide). Label reactants (left) and products (right).
topics.exemplar: Write the word equation for methane burning in oxygen and label reactants and products.

topics.src: Study Pack §1 A Q4-5; Extract §SCIENCE model 1
topics.grounding: Mass of reactants = mass of products (mass not created/destroyed). Closed system: mass constant. Open system: a gas product escapes so measured mass drops. Calc style: add reactant masses to get product mass (14.8+34.8=49.6g); or start-final = gas lost (10+15-24=1g).
topics.exemplar: 10 g magnesium in 15 g hydrochloric acid produces hydrogen gas; the solution then weighs 24 g. How much hydrogen gas was released?

topics.src: Study Pack §1 A Q6-7; Extract model 2
topics.grounding: Synthesis: 2+ reactants combine into one (A+B->AB). Decomposition: one reactant breaks into 2+ products (AB->A+B), e.g. 2H2O2->2H2O+O2, CaCO3->CaO+CO2. Justify by counting reactants/products. Balancing: change the big numbers in front only, never subscripts.
topics.exemplar: Elephant's toothpaste is hydrogen peroxide breaking into water and oxygen. What reaction type is it and how do you know?

topics.src: Study Pack §1 A Q8; Extract §SCIENCE corrosion
topics.grounding: Corrosion/rusting = metal degrading. Needs ALL of iron + oxygen + water. Word eq: iron + oxygen + water -> hydrated iron oxide (rust). It is a synthesis reaction. Prevent: paint; oil/grease/plastic coat; galvanise (zinc, more reactive); sacrificial metal; keep dry.
topics.exemplar: What conditions are needed for rusting, and give two ways to prevent it.

topics.src: Study Pack §1 A Q9; Extract model 3
topics.grounding: Ionic = metal + non-metal, TRANSFER electrons, form lattices of charged ions (NaCl, CaCO3). Covalent = non-metal + non-metal, SHARE electrons, form molecules (H2O, CO2, O2). Metallic = a metal alone. Both ionic & covalent fill outer shells for stability.
topics.exemplar: Compare ionic and covalent bonding with an example of each.

topics.grounding: Soluble: nitrates, group-1 (Na/K) salts, most chlorides. Insoluble: most carbonates & hydroxides (except group 1); sulfates insoluble for barium & lead. e.g. barium sulfate insoluble; potassium chloride soluble; aluminium hydroxide insoluble.
topics.exemplar: Is barium sulfate soluble or insoluble?

topics.grounding: Two soluble salts react and swap partners (AB+CD->AD+CB); the precipitate is whichever product is insoluble. e.g. lithium carbonate + barium nitrate -> barium carbonate (precipitate) + lithium nitrate.
topics.exemplar: Magnesium chloride + sodium hydroxide react. Name the products and which is the precipitate.

topics.grounding: Continental drift: continents were joined and drifted apart. Wegener's evidence: jigsaw fit of coastlines, matching rocks, mountains and fossils across oceans; supercontinent Pangaea. Dismissed because he couldn't explain the MECHANISM (what moved them); he wasn't a geologist.
topics.exemplar: Describe Wegener's theory, his evidence, and why it was dismissed at first.

topics.grounding: Convergent: plates move together; crust compresses or subducts; forms mountains, trenches, volcanic islands. Divergent: plates move apart; crust rifts or magma rises to make new crust; forms mid-ocean ridges. Transform: slide past; strong earthquakes, no volcanoes. Convection currents in the mantle drive plates.
topics.exemplar: Distinguish between a convergent and a divergent plate boundary and the features formed at each.

topics.src: Study Pack §1 B (fault types); paper_only for drawing
topics.grounding: Normal fault: tension (pulled apart), hanging wall drops. Reverse fault: compression (pushed together), hanging wall rises. Strike-slip: blocks slide sideways. (Diagrams are paper-only.)
topics.exemplar: Describe what happens at a normal fault.

topics.grounding: Oceanic crust: thinner, denser, younger (basalt), subducts. Continental: thicker, less dense, older (granite). Volcanoes at convergent/divergent boundaries. Earthquake hazards: shaking, building collapse, tsunamis, landslides, fires.
topics.exemplar: Compare oceanic and continental crust.

topics.grounding: Seafloor spreading: new crust at the ridge (youngest), pushed outwards, so rock gets older away from the ridge. Rate = distance / time; 1 km = 100,000 cm. e.g. 936 km old 72,000,000 yr -> 93,600,000 cm / 72,000,000 = 1.3 cm/yr.
topics.exemplar: A strip of seafloor is 936 km from the ridge and 72 million years old. Calculate the spreading rate in cm/year.

topics.src: Study Pack §1 C skills list; Extract §SCIENCE variables
topics.grounding: Hypothesis: 'If [IV changes], then [DV will...]'. Independent variable = what you change; dependent = what you measure; controlled = kept the same (list several). Reliability = repeat >=3 times for consistent results. Validity = fair test, measures what it should, only IV changed.
topics.exemplar: A student tests if warmer water dissolves sugar faster. Write a hypothesis and state the independent, dependent and a controlled variable.

topics.grounding: Describe a trend mentioning BOTH variables (e.g. 'as time increased, temperature increased then levelled off'). Interpolate = read a value between data points; extrapolate = beyond. Bar graph for categorical IV, line graph for continuous IV. A valid conclusion restates the result referring to the data.
topics.exemplar: Given a table of time vs temperature, describe the trend (both variables) and estimate a value between two points.

topics.src: Study Pack §2 T1; Extract §HISTORY Pearl Harbour
topics.grounding: 7 Dec 1941 Japan attacked the US naval base at Pearl Harbour (Hawaii). Reasons: cripple the US Pacific Fleet so it couldn't stop Japanese expansion; secure resources (oil) and territory across SE Asia/Pacific; response to US sanctions/oil embargo. Consequence: brought the USA into the war -> ultimately Japan's defeat.
topics.exemplar: Give two reasons why Japan attacked Pearl Harbour.

topics.src: Study Pack §2 T2; Extract §HISTORY Fall of Singapore
topics.grounding: Feb 1942 Singapore (major British base) fell to Japan; shattered Australia's security and shifted alliance to the USA. Propaganda posters 'He's Coming South', 'Ringed with Menace' created panic/urgency to enlist and support the war.
topics.exemplar: Explain how Japanese expansion changed Australia's sense of security in 1942 and how propaganda was used.

topics.grounding: Lark Force (Rabaul): defeated Jan 1942; ~1,050 prisoners died when the Montevideo Maru was torpedoed. Gull Force (Ambon): Laha Massacre, 300+ killed; ~80% of the force died in captivity. Sparrow Force (Timor): commandos fought a year-long guerrilla war ('They alone did not surrender').
topics.exemplar: Describe what happened to one of the forces defending Australia's north.

topics.grounding: 1929 Geneva Convention required humane treatment, food/shelter/medical care, safe non-military work, communication, protection from punishment, Red Cross inspections. Japanese death rate ~27% vs ~4% German/Italian. They breached the Convention: starvation, forced labour, beatings, no medical care.
topics.exemplar: Did the Japanese treat POWs in line with the Geneva Convention? Justify.

topics.grounding: Thai-Burma 'Death' Railway: 415 km, Ban Pong (Thailand) to Thanbyuzayat (Burma); built because sea supply was too dangerous after Midway. ~13,000 of ~60,000 Allied POWs were Australian; 'Hellfire Pass'; 1943 'Speedo' 18-hr shifts; watery-rice rations; cholera/dysentery/malaria; 'Weary' Dunlop. 2,800+ Australians died; F Force ~44% death rate.
topics.exemplar: Describe a major challenge POWs faced on the Thai-Burma Railway (challenge -> effect -> example -> impact).

topics.grounding: Darwin first bombed 19 Feb 1942 (bombing continued to Nov 1943). Significant: first attack on the Australian mainland; shocked the nation; showed Australia directly under threat.
topics.exemplar: When was Darwin first bombed and why was it significant?

topics.grounding: Kokoda Trail (Port Moresby to Buna): Australians/Papuans halted the Japanese advance on Port Moresby. Challenges: extreme mountain terrain, mud, jungle, disease, supply difficulty over the Owen Stanley Range. 'Fuzzy Wuzzy Angels' = Papuan carriers who carried supplies/wounded. Importance: crucial defensive victory protecting Australia.
topics.exemplar: Why was the Kokoda campaign important for Australia?

topics.src: Study Pack §2 T8; Extract §HISTORY Indigenous service
topics.grounding: Aboriginal & Torres Strait Islander service (stated to be on the exam): legislative restrictions on enlistment; often segregated units/support roles; discrimination; after the war frequently denied the same recognition, pay, land or benefits as other veterans.
topics.exemplar: Name one way Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander WWII service was treated differently.

sections.name: Section II — Short answers
sections.style: 5 structured short answers (4-6 marks), Changing Places / Dee Why

exam.src: Study Pack §3 (30 marks: Section I MC 10, Section II short 20)

topics.grounding: Economic restructuring = shift from manufacturing to service/knowledge industries. Urban consolidation = higher density in existing suburbs (apartments/infill) to cut sprawl. Urban renewal = redeveloping decayed areas. Urban sprawl = outward low-density spread. Gentrification = higher-income residents move in, raising prices and changing character. Urbanisation = rising share living in cities.
topics.exemplar: Define urban consolidation.

topics.grounding: Liveability = quality of life based on environmental, social and economic factors. Indicators (5 Ds): Density, Diversity of use/income, Design, Distance to transit, Destination access. Judged with social/economic/environmental indicators.
topics.exemplar: Define liveability and name three indicators used to judge it.

topics.src: Extract §GEOGRAPHY rate of change; Study Pack §3 data skills
topics.grounding: % change = (new - old) / old x 100. Dee Why: rent $220->$740 = 236%; income $930->$2,640 = 184%; so rent rose faster than income -> rental stress up, affordability down. Manufacturing 17%->6% ~= -65%.
topics.exemplar: Rent rose from $220 to $740. Calculate the percentage change and state one implication.

topics.grounding: NSW plan: Eastern Harbour City (Sydney CBD), Central River City (Parramatta), Western Parkland City (Western Sydney Airport). Aims to cut sprawl, raise density and connectivity. 80% of new dwellings within the existing footprint.
topics.exemplar: Name the three cities in the Metropolis of Three Cities plan.

topics.src: Study Pack §3 Section II Q11; Extract §GEOGRAPHY drivers
topics.grounding: Why Dee Why was renewed: Metropolis of Three Cities push for density to cut sprawl; rising land value made redevelopment viable; already a central established Northern Beaches hub; partial decay of the town centre. Chain: economic restructuring -> rising land value -> population growth -> urban decay -> investment -> renewal.
topics.exemplar: Explain why Dee Why underwent urban renewal (two reasons). (4 marks)

topics.src: Study Pack §3 Section II Q12; Extract §GEOGRAPHY economic viability
topics.grounding: Local jobs +50% (2001-2024); unemployment 6.8%->2.9%; income +184% but rent +236%; only 3% of new dwellings affordable; retail vacancy 12%->3%; 30,000 m2 new retail since 2019. Shows renewal drove economic change but reduced affordability.
topics.exemplar: Using data, explain how urban renewal has caused economic change in Dee Why. (6 marks)

topics.src: Study Pack §3 Section II Q13; Extract §GEOGRAPHY environmental sustainability
topics.grounding: WSUD captures/treats/reuses stormwater; beach width +11 m, Water Quality Index 80/100. Tree canopy 15%->23% (each 10% = ~1C cooler). Limitations: 70% of canopy gain on public land, private fell 6%; 2023 storm drains blocked; Pittwater Rd traffic +21%. Walkability index 74.
topics.exemplar: Assess how effective WSUD and tree canopy have been for Dee Why's sustainability, with one limitation. (6 marks)

topics.src: Extract §GEOGRAPHY model evaluation; Study Pack §3 Section III Q16
topics.grounding: Evaluate liveability: gentrification raised investment but escalated prices (unit $340k->$1.11m) and rental stress (+19%). Transport (B-Line) and canopy improved, but social liveability (affordability) declined. Judgement: moderate economic/environmental gains, reduced social liveability. Use 3+ indicators + clear judgement + evidence.
topics.exemplar: Evaluate the extent to which urban renewal has improved overall liveability in Dee Why. (8 marks)

topics.src: Study Pack §3 practice exam Section I; Extract §GEOGRAPHY
topics.grounding: Global North restructuring: growth of service/professional sectors. Global South: increased informal employment, inequality, over-urbanisation (informal settlements, poor sanitation, congestion, infrastructure outpaced by growth). Megacity = 10m+ people.
topics.exemplar: In the Global South, restructuring and globalisation have often caused what?

sections.name: Part C — Extended response
sections.style: extended; likely 'how physical activity positively affects health'

exam.src: Study Pack §4 (50 marks: MC 15, short 25, extended 10)

topics.grounding: 5 HEALTH-related: cardiorespiratory endurance (running), muscular strength (heavy lift), muscular endurance (push-ups), flexibility (stretching), body composition (fat vs lean). 6 SKILL-related: agility, balance, coordination, power (strength x speed), reaction time, speed. Exercise = planned, structured, repetitive activity to improve fitness. Physical fitness = doing daily tasks with energy and reserves.
topics.exemplar: Describe two health-related components of fitness with an example of each.

topics.src: Study Pack §4 Q19 (the actual extended-response question)
topics.grounding: Extended response: how physical activity positively affects health. Physical: stronger heart/lungs, healthy weight, stronger bones/muscles, lower risk of heart disease/type-2 diabetes/some cancers, better sleep. Mental/emotional: endorphins, less stress/anxiety/depression, self-esteem. Social: teamwork, friendships, belonging. Guideline: 13-17 yr olds >=60 min moderate-vigorous activity daily. Use an example per point.
topics.exemplar: Explain how physical activity can positively affect the health of individuals.

topics.grounding: 6 nutrients: carbohydrates (main energy; bread/rice/pasta), protein (growth/repair building blocks; meat/eggs), fats (dense energy; unsaturated in avocado/nuts/oily fish), vitamins, minerals (calcium=bones, iron=oxygen transport), water (~60% of body, 6-8 cups/day).
topics.exemplar: Which nutrient is the building block for cell growth and repair, and name food sources?

topics.grounding: Body image = how a person sees, thinks and feels about their own body. Stereotype = oversimplified generalised belief about a group. Social norms = expected behaviours of a group. Eating disorders = serious illnesses with disturbed eating behaviours/thoughts about food, weight, body shape.
topics.exemplar: What is meant by 'body image'?

topics.grounding: Depressant = slows the central nervous system (alcohol, cannabis). Drugs classified by effect (depressant/stimulant/hallucinogen) and legal status (licit/illicit). Risk taking is a consequence of poor decision making. Illicit drugs harm individuals and families.
topics.exemplar: What is a depressant? Give an example.

topics.grounding: Primary prevention = stop a problem before it starts (school drug education, ad campaigns). Secondary = early detection/intervention (screening, counselling). Tertiary = treatment/rehabilitation (rehab, support groups). Predisposition = greater likelihood (e.g. of addiction) from genetics/family/environment.
topics.exemplar: What is primary prevention? Give an example.

topics.grounding: STI = sexually transmitted infection. Contraception = methods to prevent pregnancy (barrier methods like condoms also protect against STIs). Four classifications: barrier, hormonal, natural/behavioural, permanent/surgical.
topics.exemplar: What are the four classifications of contraception?

sections.name: Section II — Gap-fill
sections.style: circular flow: 5 sectors, 3 leakages, 3 injections; business cycle

sections.name: Section III — Short responses
sections.style: circular flow, inflation, fiscal & monetary policy

topics.grounding: Scarcity = unlimited wants but finite resources, forcing choices and trade-offs. Opportunity cost = the value of the next-best alternative given up when you choose. e.g. $20 to spend on a shirt OR a movie; choosing one gives up the other.
topics.exemplar: Define opportunity cost with an example.

topics.grounding: Inflation = sustained rise in the general price level. Unemployment = people willing and able to work but without jobs. GDP = total value of goods and services produced in a country in a year (a measure of economic performance). ('GDP — this is in the test!')
topics.exemplar: What does GDP measure?

topics.src: Study Pack §5 gap-fill; Extract §COMMERCE circular flow
topics.grounding: Circular flow 5 sectors: households, businesses/firms, government, financial sector, overseas/international. 3 LEAKAGES (withdrawals): savings, taxes, imports. 3 INJECTIONS: investment, government spending, exports. A diagram will be in the exam.
topics.exemplar: Name the three leakages and three injections in the circular flow of income.

topics.grounding: Business/economic cycle: the ups and downs of economic activity over time — boom (peak), downturn/contraction, trough (recession), recovery/upturn. Governments aim to smooth it.
topics.exemplar: Name the phases of the business cycle.

topics.grounding: Fiscal policy = the GOVERNMENT using spending and taxation to shape the economy. Expansionary (downturn): more spending + tax cuts -> injects funds, creates jobs. Contractionary (curb inflation): less spending + higher taxes -> withdrawals.
topics.exemplar: Explain how expansionary fiscal policy works.

topics.grounding: Monetary policy = the RESERVE BANK changing the cash rate (interest rates). Expansionary: lower rates -> more borrowing/spending -> injection; lower mortgage repayments raise disposable income. Contractionary: higher rates -> less spending -> curbs inflation but can slow growth.
topics.exemplar: Explain how the Reserve Bank uses monetary policy to slow inflation.

sections.name: Section III — Structured response
sections.style: school scaffold: Topic -> linking word -> knowledge (Is.../Occurs.../Causes.../Avoided by...). Key topics: handwashing, cleaning & sanitising, FIFO

topics.grounding: Danger zone = 5 C to 60 C, where bacteria grow and multiply. Affects perishable foods (raw meat, dairy). Causes food poisoning. Avoid by storing perishables at 4 C or below. Example: raw chicken left on the bench too long.
topics.exemplar: Explain why it is important to keep food out of the danger zone.

topics.grounding: Cross contamination = bacteria transferred from one object/food to another, esp. raw to cooked. Occurs via the same knife/board for raw and cooked. Causes food poisoning (vomiting, diarrhoea, cramps). Avoid with colour-coded boards (yellow raw chicken, brown cooked) and washing knives.
topics.exemplar: Identify and explain how cross contamination can occur in a commercial kitchen.

topics.grounding: Handwashing: wet, soap, scrub 20s (palms, backs, between fingers, nails), rinse, dry with paper towel; before handling food, after raw meat/toilet/face. Cleaning = remove visible dirt with hot water + detergent; Sanitising = reduce bacteria with sanitiser/very hot water, AFTER cleaning. Order: scrape, wash, rinse, sanitise, air dry.
topics.exemplar: Describe the difference between cleaning and sanitising, and the correct order.

topics.grounding: FIFO = First In, First Out: oldest stock used first. New deliveries go behind/under older stock; label with dates. Prevents food passing its use-by date, reduces waste, saves money. Example: new milk to the back of the cool room.
topics.exemplar: What is FIFO stock rotation and why is it used?

topics.grounding: Types of new products: LINE EXTENSION (new variant of an existing product, e.g. a new flavour), NEW-TO-WORLD (a genuinely new product), ME-TOO (a copy of a competitor's product). Reasons to develop: new markets, trends, tech, profit.
topics.exemplar: Distinguish between line extension, new-to-world and me-too products.

topics.grounding: Six nutrients: carbohydrates, protein, fats, vitamins, minerals, water. Macronutrients (carbs/protein/fats) needed in large amounts; micronutrients (vitamins/minerals) in small amounts. Each has a function and food sources (see PDHPE nutrients).
topics.exemplar: Name the six essential nutrients and classify them as macro or micro.

topics.grounding: Bush foods = native Australian foods used traditionally by Aboriginal peoples and increasingly in modern cuisine (e.g. Davidson's plum - high in vitamin E, zinc, a dairy-free calcium source). Topics: consumption patterns, traditional vs modern uses.
topics.exemplar: Give an example of a bush food and one of its nutritional benefits.
